payoff: Two game families and future family games cease commercialization by contract
exact_locked_narration: Light & Wonder paid Aristocrat one hundred and twenty-seven point five million dollars to settle Dragon Train. But the deal also barred commercialization of Dragon Train and Jewel of the Dragon worldwide—including future games in both families. Not a criminal fine. Not a jury award.

payoff: Metadata clue, not final finding of copied formulas
exact_locked_narration: In a preliminary ruling, a federal judge described a Light & Wonder Sky Train development worksheet dated November twelfth, 2013. An older Aristocrat workbook carried the same creation date. The match raised questions about origin—not a final verdict that Dragon Train copied every calculation.

payoff: Some probabilities observable, other math still raises serious trade secret issues
exact_locked_narration: In a preliminary Dragon Train ruling, a federal judge partly agreed with Light & Wonder: some bonus-symbol probabilities could be inferred from visible gameplay. But other mathematical combinations still raised serious trade-secret concerns. That partial defense argument did not clear the company of the broader claim.

payoff: Commercial restriction survives through negotiated settlement contract
exact_locked_narration: In February 2026, a federal court vacated temporary injunctions against Light & Wonder. So why couldn't Dragon Train and Jewel of the Dragon be commercialized? A settlement contract separately prohibited commercialization of both game families. The court orders ended, but the contractual restriction survived.
